builder_plan.scenario: A support or data assistant repeats work across related customer requests.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's memory change in a replay of past tasks, with separate memory per customer.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current memory pipeline plus a no-memory control using the same agent.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, stale memories, retrieval misses, response latency, and all memory maintenance costs.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
summary: Replaces flat, lesson-only agent memory (insights distilled from trajectories and later injected without provenance) with lessons linked to per-trajectory success/failure summaries and raw trajectories, letting the agent verify or correct a lesson before acting. Costs include storing trajectories alongside insights, extra retrieval and terminal-tool calls to descend through links when lessons conflict, lack detail, or originate from failed tasks, which adds latency, token spend, and pipeline complexity. Failure modes include corrupted or missing raw trajectories, high retrieval overhead on large memory stores, and residual degradation when summaries omit the evidence needed to catch a wrong lesson.
rationale: The verification mechanism is implementable on constrained infrastructure as a storage-plus-prompting change, but its benefit must be validated against plain lesson memory on the reader's specific tasks since gains are benchmark-relative, not absolute.

claims.statement: Replaces flat, lesson-only agent memory (insights distilled from trajectories and later injected without provenance) with lessons linked to per-trajectory success/failure summaries and raw trajectories, letting the agent verify or correct a lesson before acting. Costs include storing trajectories alongside insights, extra retrieval and terminal-tool calls to descend through links when lessons conflict, lack detail, or originate from failed tasks, which adds latency, token spend, and pipeline complexity. Failure modes include corrupted or missing raw trajectories, high retrieval overhead on large memory stores, and residual degradation when summaries omit the evidence needed to catch a wrong lesson.

Consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a same-insights baseline across five agentic benchmarks, while reducing memory-induced degradation; no single quantified factor is reported in the abstract.
